s0.title: Give OpsWatch its own AWS identity
s0.purpose: OpsWatch needs an identity whose only right is to assume the read-only roles you will create in the next steps.

tabs.server: OpsWatch runs on my computer or a server (Docker)
tabs.aws: OpsWatch runs on AWS (ECS or EC2)

server.i1: Sign in to the AWS console of the account where you want to keep OpsWatch's identity. It can be the account you will monitor.
server.i2: Open IAM → Users → "Create user". Name it opswatch. Leave "Provide user access to the AWS Management Console" unchecked, then click "Next".
server.i3: On "<ui>Set permissions</ui>", keep "<ui>Add user to group</ui>" or choose "<ui>Attach policies directly</ui>" without selecting any policy. Click "<ui>Next</ui>", then "<ui>Create user</ui>".
server.i4: Open the new user → "Permissions" tab → "Add permissions" → "Create inline policy" → "JSON" tab. Replace the content with the policy below, click "Next", name it OpsWatchAssumeRole, then click "Create policy".
server.i5: Open the "<ui>Security credentials</ui>" tab → "<ui>Create access key</ui>" → use case "<ui>Application running outside AWS</ui>" → "<ui>Next</ui>" → "<ui>Create access key</ui>". Copy the "<ui>Access key</ui>" and the "<ui>Secret access key</ui>": the secret is shown only once.
server.i6: In OpsWatch's .env file, set AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY to these two values, and AWS_REGION to your usual region, for example eu-west-1. Check that OPSWATCH_SECRET holds at least 32 random characters (generate them with openssl rand -base64 48): without it, OpsWatch refuses to start. Then restart OpsWatch with docker compose up -d.
server.profileTitle: Docker: keys in .env, profiles for npm run dev
server.profile: With Docker, put AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY in .env. An AWS CLI profile (aws configure --profile opswatch, then AWS_PROFILE=opswatch) is meant for npm run dev: the container runs as user 1001 and usually cannot read a mounted ~/.aws/credentials file, whose mode is 600, and SSO profiles also need a writable cache. If the two key variables and AWS_PROFILE are all set, OpsWatch uses the keys and logs a warning at startup.
server.i7: Check: once you have created the connection in step 1, its page no longer warns that OpsWatch has no AWS identity. The "{identityTitle}" card shows the ARN of the opswatch user.

aws.i1: ECS: open the task definition and note the "<ui>Task role</ui>" (not the "<ui>Task execution role</ui>"). EC2: open the instance → "<ui>Security</ui>" tab → note the "<ui>IAM Role</ui>". If there is none, create a role for the ECS task or the EC2 service and attach it.
aws.i2: Open IAM → Roles → that role → "Add permissions" → "Create inline policy" → "JSON". Paste the policy below, click "Next", name it OpsWatchAssumeRole, then click "Create policy".
aws.i3: Redeploy the ECS service ("Update service" → "Force new deployment") or restart OpsWatch on the instance so it picks up the role. There are no keys to configure: leave AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and AWS_PROFILE empty.

sso.title: What about IAM Identity Center (SSO)?
sso.body: Use IAM, not IAM Identity Center. Identity Center is made for people who sign in: its credentials are temporary and expire after a few hours, so OpsWatch would stop working until someone runs aws sso login again. For a tool that runs all the time, use an IAM user or an ECS or EC2 role. For a quick local try, an SSO profile set through AWS_PROFILE works until the session expires.

ownKey.title: Why not use my own access key?
ownKey.body: It works, but it is not recommended. Your key usually has administrator rights: if OpsWatch's .env, server or database leaks, the whole account is exposed. The dedicated identity can only assume {rolePattern} roles, which are read-only. You can revoke it without touching your own access, and CloudTrail shows clearly what OpsWatch did. Never create access keys for the root user.

s1.title: Create the connection in OpsWatch
s1.purpose: The connection records the account to monitor and generates the unique values its CloudFormation template needs.
s1.i3: Fill in "<ui>{name}</ui>", "<ui>{accountId}</ui>" (the 12 digits of the account to monitor, shown in the account menu at the top right of the AWS console) and "<ui>{regions}</ui>" (the regions where your resources run).
s1.i4: Click "<ui>{submit}</ui>". OpsWatch creates a unique ExternalId and prepares the template for this connection.

s2.title: Deploy the CloudFormation stack in the account to monitor
s2.purpose: The stack creates the read-only role that OpsWatch will assume. Choose one of the three ways below.
s2.region: Create the stack in one region only. IAM is global, so any region works.

console.title: With the AWS console
console.i1: On the OpsWatch connection page, click "<ui>{download}</ui>".
console.i2: In the AWS console of the account to monitor, open <ui>CloudFormation</ui> → <ui>Stacks</ui> → "<ui>Create stack</ui>" → "<ui>With new resources (standard)</ui>".
console.i3: Choose "<ui>Upload a template file</ui>" → "<ui>Choose file</ui>", select the downloaded file, then click "<ui>Next</ui>".
console.i4: In "Stack name", enter {stackName}: the name of the downloaded file without .yaml, also shown in the AWS CLI command of the connection page. Click "Next", then "Next" again.
console.i5: On "<ui>Review and create</ui>", tick "<ui>I acknowledge that AWS CloudFormation might create IAM resources with custom names.</ui>", then click "<ui>Submit</ui>".
console.i6: Wait for the status CREATE_COMPLETE, which takes about one minute.

cli.title: With the AWS CLI
cli.i1: On the connection page, click "<ui>{download}</ui>" and copy the AWS CLI command shown below the button.
cli.i2: Run it from the folder containing the downloaded template, with credentials of the account to monitor. It already contains --capabilities CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM, the command-line equivalent of the acknowledgement box.

launch.title: With Launch Stack (experimental)
launch.note: Experimental: this option has not yet been validated against a real AWS account. Only available when OPSWATCH_TEMPLATE_BUCKET is configured. OpsWatch uploads the template to that bucket, so its identity needs s3:PutObject on it, and the console user of the monitored account must be able to read the template object: allow it with a bucket policy granting s3:GetObject on opswatch/templates/*. When in doubt, download the template instead.
launch.i1: On the connection page, click "<ui>{launchStack}</ui>". The AWS console opens with the template and the stack name already filled in.
launch.i2: Tick the acknowledgement box, then click "<ui>Create stack</ui>".

s3.title: Paste the role ARN
s3.purpose: The ARN tells OpsWatch which role to assume in the monitored account.
s3.i1: In CloudFormation, open the stack → "Outputs" tab → copy the value of RoleArn. It looks like {example}.
s3.i2: On the connection page, paste it into "<ui>{roleArnLabel}</ui>" and click "<ui>{save}</ui>".

s4.title: Run the test
s4.purpose: OpsWatch assumes the role and checks, service by service, what it can read.
s4.i1: On the connection page, click "<ui>{run}</ui>". The result appears after a few seconds.
s4.i2: Read the colour of each line:
s4.green: <ui>Green, "{status}"</ui>: OpsWatch can read this service. Nothing to do.
s4.orange: <ui>Orange, "{status}"</ui>: an action is missing and the line says what you lose. Open "<services>{servicesTitle}</services>" to see why OpsWatch needs it, then add it by updating the stack with a newly downloaded template.
s4.red: <ui>Red</ui>: the connection or the check failed, and the message gives the reason. See "<troubleshooting>{troubleshootingTitle}</troubleshooting>".

ambient.title: Running on AWS
ambient.intro: OpsWatch runs on ECS or EC2 in the account it monitors and reads it with its own task or instance role: no stack and no keys.

s1.title: Find the role OpsWatch runs with
s1.purpose: This role will receive the read-only permissions.

s2.title: Attach the read-only policy
s2.i1: Open <ui>IAM</ui> → <ui>Roles</ui> → that role → "<ui>Add permissions</ui>" → "<ui>Create inline policy</ui>" → "<ui>JSON</ui>".

s3.title: Restart OpsWatch
s3.purpose: A restart makes sure OpsWatch runs with the role and its new permissions.
s3.i1: ECS: open the service → "Update service" → "Force new deployment". EC2: restart OpsWatch on the instance, for example with docker compose restart.

s4.title: Create the connection and run the test
s4.purpose: OpsWatch checks that its role can read the account.
s4.i2: Choose "<ui>{method}</ui>". In "<ui>{accountId}</ui>", enter the ID of the account OpsWatch runs in: this method cannot read another account.
s4.i3: Select the regions and click "<ui>{submit}</ui>", then click "<ui>{run}</ui>" on the connection page.

keys.title: With access keys
keys.intro: For a quick local test. The keys belong to a dedicated read-only user, never to your own IAM user or to the root user.

s1.title: Create a dedicated IAM user
s1.purpose: This user can only read, so a leaked key cannot change anything in your account.
s1.i1: In the AWS console of the account to monitor, open <ui>IAM</ui> → <ui>Users</ui> → "<ui>Create user</ui>".
s1.i2: Name it opswatch-readonly and leave "Provide user access to the AWS Management Console" unchecked. Click "Next", "Next" again, then "Create user".

s2.title: Attach the read-only policy
s2.i1: Open the new user → "<ui>Permissions</ui>" tab → "<ui>Add permissions</ui>" → "<ui>Create inline policy</ui>" → "<ui>JSON</ui>" tab.

s3.title: Create an access key
s3.purpose: OpsWatch signs its AWS requests with this key pair.
s3.i1: Open the "<ui>Security credentials</ui>" tab → "<ui>Create access key</ui>" → use case "<ui>Application running outside AWS</ui>" → "<ui>Next</ui>" → "<ui>Create access key</ui>".
s3.i2: Copy the "<ui>Access key</ui>" and the "<ui>Secret access key</ui>". The secret is shown only once.

s4.title: Save the keys in OpsWatch
s4.purpose: OpsWatch encrypts the keys before storing them.
s4.i2: Choose "<ui>{method}</ui>", fill in the name, the account ID and the regions, then click "<ui>{submit}</ui>".
s4.i3: On the connection page, paste the values into "<ui>{accessKeyId}</ui>" and "<ui>{secretAccessKey}</ui>", then click "<ui>{save}</ui>".
s4.i4: The keys are encrypted and never shown again: only a hint like AKIA…MPLE remains.

s5.title: Run the test and look after the key
s5.purpose: A long-lived key needs care for as long as it exists.
s5.i2: Rotate the key regularly: create a new one, save it in OpsWatch, then delete the old one in IAM.
s5.i3: Delete the key in IAM when you stop using OpsWatch, and switch to the <role>IAM role method</role> whenever you can.

GettingStarted.servicesIntro: The role is deliberately narrower than the AWS ReadOnlyAccess policy, which can read the content of S3 buckets. OpsWatch never reads S3, Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store.

pages.title: What OpsWatch shows
pages.intro: Once a connection passes its permission test, pick it in the top bar, then a region, to open these pages.

items.overview: Overview: health summary and automatic insights (tasks below desired over 10 minutes; high CPU or memory, failed deployments, database CPU and memory, Aurora replica lag, load balancer 5xx errors and unhealthy hosts, alarms firing, over 15 minutes).
items.containers: Containers: ECS services with tasks, CPU and memory, then per service its charts, tasks, events, target groups and log groups.
items.databases: Databases: RDS and Aurora instances with their role, metrics and, when Performance Insights is on, the top SQL statements.
items.loadBalancers: Load balancers: requests, 5xx errors, p95 response time and target health of each application load balancer.
items.alarms: Alarms: CloudWatch alarms by state, with target-tracking autoscaling alarms hidden by default.
items.logs: Logs: pick log groups and run CloudWatch Logs Insights queries over up to 24 hours, with example queries for errors, 5xx responses and slow requests.

pages.refresh: Charts cover 1 hour to 7 days and refresh every 2 minutes while the tab is visible; you can pause the refresh.

security.title: Security
security.can1: Read the metadata and metrics of the services listed above.
security.can2: Run the Logs Insights queries you start, which AWS bills.
security.cannot1: Change, create or delete anything in your account.
security.cannot2: Read S3 objects, secrets or parameters.
security.cannot3: Be assumed by any AWS identity other than this OpsWatch instance's: the trust policy names it.
security.externalIdBody: The trust policy already limits the role to this OpsWatch instance's AWS identity, so learning the role ARN is not enough to use it. The ExternalId covers two remaining cases: several OpsWatch instances or tenants sharing one base identity, where one could be pointed at another's role (the confused deputy problem), and a connection configured with the role of another connection. The role only accepts requests that also present the random value generated for its own connection.
security.revokeBody: Delete the CloudFormation stack. The role disappears and OpsWatch loses access immediately. Then remove the connection in OpsWatch.

assumeRole.title: AccessDenied when assuming the role
assumeRole.body: The trust policy does not match: the stack was deployed from an older template, the ExternalId was regenerated, or OpsWatch now runs with another identity. Download the template again and update the stack.

region.title: A region always fails
region.body: The region may be disabled for your account. Enable it in the AWS account settings, or remove it from the connection.

pi.title: Performance Insights is "not applicable"
pi.body: No instance in that region has Performance Insights enabled. Enable it on the database instance to get the top SQL.

scp.title: A permission stays missing although the role has it
scp.body: A service control policy (SCP) of your AWS organization or a permissions boundary may deny the action. Ask your organization administrator.

account.title: The credentials belong to another account
account.body: The role ARN or the keys come from another AWS account than the one entered for the connection. Check the 12-digit account ID.

hub.title: Connect the systems you use
hub.subtitle: OpsWatch reads what you already run and tells you when something is wrong. Start with whichever of these you have.
hub.intro: Most installations begin with AWS, because that is where the services, databases and load balancers are. The others make what OpsWatch finds easier to act on — none of them is required, and each says plainly what it adds.
hub.guidesIntro: Each guide covers what the integration unlocks, what it needs, exactly what OpsWatch is allowed to do with it, and how to take it away again.

unlocks.aws: Services, databases, load balancers, alarms, logs, errors and deployments. This is the monitoring itself.
unlocks.github: Turns a stack frame into a link to the file it came from, and tells you which commits a deployment carried.
unlocks.cloudflare: Traffic, cache and security events at the edge, for the zones you choose.
unlocks.ai: Optional. Lets a model narrate what OpsWatch already measured. Nothing else depends on it.

github.title: Connect GitHub
github.subtitle: So that a problem can tell you what changed.
github.chainLabel: How a problem reaches the code that caused it

0.title: Service
0.detail: An ECS service OpsWatch already watches.

1.title: Repository
1.detail: You map the service to the repository that builds it.

2.title: Deployment
2.detail: The collector records each rollout of that service.

3.title: Commit
3.detail: OpsWatch reads the commits between one rollout and the last.

4.title: Changed files
4.detail: Paths and line counts for each of those commits.

5.title: Problem
5.detail: A problem that opened after the rollout is shown beside it, with the gap stated.

unlocks.title: What connecting GitHub adds
unlocks.intro: Without it, OpsWatch can tell you a service broke twelve minutes after a deployment. With it, it can also tell you which commits that deployment carried and which files they touched — and link a stack frame to the file it came from.

before.title: Before you start
before.intro: Two things, and neither is a surprise later.
before.needDetail: A GitHub account that can see the repositories your services are built from, and permission to create a fine-grained personal access token for them.
before.costDetail: Nothing. OpsWatch makes a handful of read requests per deployment, bounded at ten commits and twenty files each, and stores the result so a page never calls GitHub.

permissions.title: What OpsWatch is allowed to do
permissions.intro: Read your repositories. That is the whole of it.
permissions.grantDetail: Contents: Read and Metadata: Read, scoped to the repositories you want OpsWatch to know about. Nothing else is needed and nothing else is used.
permissions.whyDetail: Metadata names the repository and its default branch, so a link points at the right place. Contents reads the commit list and the files each commit changed. Neither can alter anything.
permissions.guaranteeTitle: Why read-only is more than a promise here
permissions.guaranteeDetail: OpsWatch's GitHub client contains no write request — not a create, not an update, not a delete. A token that happens to carry write permission would still only ever be used to read, because there is no code that could do otherwise. A test asserts that absence, so it cannot quietly change.

steps.title: Connecting it
steps.methodIntro: Five steps, and you can stop after the third — a verified token already links stack frames to files.

token.title: Create a fine-grained token in GitHub
token.purpose: A fine-grained token is scoped to the repositories you pick, so OpsWatch cannot see the rest of your account.
token.body: In GitHub, open Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens, and create one. Choose only the repositories your services are built from, and set Repository permissions → Contents to Read-only and Metadata to Read-only. Copy the token: GitHub shows it once.

store.title: Paste it into OpsWatch
store.purpose: It is encrypted before it is stored, with a key derived for this purpose alone.
store.body: Open Settings → Repositories and paste the token. It is never sent back to your browser afterwards — the field stays empty, and leaving it empty keeps whatever is already stored. An AI key or an AWS credential cannot be decrypted by the same derivation, so one leak is not all of them.

verify.title: Verify it
verify.purpose: A saved token is not a working token, and OpsWatch will not pretend otherwise.
verify.body: Press Verify token. OpsWatch asks GitHub who the token belongs to and shows the account name. Until it does, the connection reads "Saved, not verified" everywhere it appears.

discover.title: Find your repositories
discover.purpose: So you pick from what exists rather than typing an owner and a name.
discover.body: Press Find repositories. OpsWatch lists what the token can see, with the default branch GitHub reports for each. Tick the ones you want recorded and save. The branch matters: a repository recorded against a branch that does not exist builds links to files nobody can open.

map.title: Map a service to a repository
map.purpose: This is the link that turns a deployment into a list of commits.
map.body: Open a problem on the service, or its error detail, and accept the repository OpsWatch suggests — or correct it. Mapping is never applied automatically: a wrong mapping sends somebody to the wrong diff during an incident, which is worse than no mapping at all.

states.title: What good and not-quite-right look like
states.intro: The Integrations page, the Accounts page and this guide all read the same state, so they cannot disagree.
states.goodDetail: The token is verified and at least one repository is recorded. Deployment details start listing commits on the next collector cycle, and stack frames link to files at the commit the error followed.
states.degradedDetail: Usually a token that has never been verified, or repositories recorded without a token. The second is a real, useful state: links to files work and file contents do not, and the page says which.

failures.title: When it does not work
failures.intro: OpsWatch never shows you GitHub's own error text — it can quote your token back — so it names the cause in its own words.

unauthorized.title: GitHub refused the token
unauthorized.fix: It has expired, been revoked, or was pasted incompletely. Create a new one and replace it; the old one is deleted when you do.

forbidden.title: The token is valid but lacks a permission
forbidden.fix: Add Contents: Read and Metadata: Read to the token's repository permissions. OpsWatch tells this apart from a rate limit, because they are fixed differently.

rateLimited.title: GitHub is rate-limiting the token
rateLimited.fix: Wait a few minutes. OpsWatch reads at most ten commits per deployment and five deployments per cycle, so this is usually another tool sharing the token.

noRepositories.title: Find repositories returns nothing
noRepositories.fix: The token is scoped to no repository, or to repositories the account cannot see. Edit its Repository access in GitHub.

wrongBranch.title: File links open a 404
wrongBranch.fix: The repository is recorded against a branch that does not exist. Re-run Find repositories: OpsWatch records the default branch GitHub reports rather than one you typed.

manage.title: Changing or removing it later
manage.intro: Everything is reversible from Settings → Repositories.
manage.disconnectDetail: The token is deleted, not flagged — a row kept with its secret would be something you asked OpsWatch to forget and it did not. Your repositories and mappings stay, because links to files and service mapping work without a token. Reconnect by pasting a new one.

cloudflare.title: Connect Cloudflare
cloudflare.subtitle: So that what happens at the edge is part of the picture.
cloudflare.chainLabel: How a Cloudflare connection is made

0.title: Token
0.detail: You create a read-only API token in Cloudflare and paste it here.

1.title: Verification
1.detail: OpsWatch asks Cloudflare whether the token works, and says so.

2.title: Zones
2.detail: It lists the zones the token can see.

3.title: Your choice
3.detail: Only the zones you tick are read. Nothing else is touched.

unlocks.title: What connecting Cloudflare adds
unlocks.intro: OpsWatch sees your infrastructure from the inside. Cloudflare sees what reached it. Connecting the two is how a quiet load balancer and a spike in blocked requests stop being separate stories.

before.title: Before you start
before.intro: One token, and a decision about scope.
before.needDetail: A Cloudflare account with at least one zone, and permission to create an API token for it.
before.costDetail: Nothing. The reads are within Cloudflare's included API allowance, and OpsWatch reads only the zones you choose.

permissions.title: What OpsWatch is allowed to do
permissions.intro: Read the zones you pick. It cannot change a setting, purge a cache or edit a rule.
permissions.grantDetail: Zone → Zone → Read, and Zone → Analytics → Read, scoped to the zones you want watched. No write permission is needed.
permissions.whyDetail: Zone: Read names your zones so you can choose from a list instead of pasting an identifier. Analytics: Read is what traffic, cache and security-event figures come from.
permissions.guaranteeDetail: The token carries the permissions you gave it, and OpsWatch then reads only the zones you ticked here. A token that can see forty zones does not put forty zones on a page — that would show somebody else's traffic to a reader who never asked for it.

steps.title: Connecting it
steps.methodIntro: Five steps. Nothing is read until the last one.

token.title: Create an API token in Cloudflare
token.purpose: Scoped to the zones you want OpsWatch to see, and to reading them.
token.body: In Cloudflare, open My Profile → API Tokens → Create Token, and start from a custom token. Add Zone → Zone → Read and Zone → Analytics → Read, then set Zone Resources to the specific zones you want watched. Copy the token: Cloudflare shows it once.

store.title: Paste it into OpsWatch
store.purpose: It is encrypted before it is stored, with a key derived for this purpose alone.
store.body: Open Settings → Cloudflare and paste the token. It is never sent back to your browser — the field stays empty afterwards. The derivation is Cloudflare's own, so a code path handling an AWS credential or an AI key cannot read it.

verify.title: Verify it
verify.purpose: A saved token is not a working token.
verify.body: Press Verify token. OpsWatch asks Cloudflare whether it is live and records the answer. Until it passes, the connection reads "Saved, not verified" on every page that mentions it.

discover.title: Find your zones
discover.purpose: So you choose from what exists rather than pasting a zone identifier.
discover.body: Press Find zones. OpsWatch lists what the token can see, with each zone's status. If the list is empty, the token is scoped to no zone — edit its Zone Resources in Cloudflare.

choose.title: Choose what to read
choose.purpose: This is the step that decides what OpsWatch actually looks at.
choose.body: Tick the zones you want and save. Until at least one is ticked the connection is verified and reads nothing, and OpsWatch says exactly that rather than claiming to be connected. Changing the selection later never disturbs the token.

states.title: What good and not-quite-right look like
states.intro: The same state appears on this guide, the Integrations page and the Accounts page. They read one source.
states.goodDetail: The token is verified and at least one zone is chosen. The connection is ready for the edge figures as they land.
states.degradedDetail: Either the token has never been verified, or it is verified and no zone is chosen. The second reads nothing at all, which is why it is not called connected.

failures.title: When it does not work
failures.intro: Cloudflare's own error text never reaches OpsWatch's pages — it can quote a token's identifier — so failures are named in OpsWatch's words.

unauthorized.title: Cloudflare refused the token
unauthorized.fix: It has expired, been rolled, or was pasted incompletely. Create a new one and replace it.

forbidden.title: The token is valid but lacks a permission
forbidden.fix: Add Zone → Analytics → Read. OpsWatch distinguishes this from a rate limit, because waiting will not fix it.

rateLimited.title: Cloudflare is rate-limiting the token
rateLimited.fix: Wait a few minutes. If it persists, another tool is probably sharing the token.

noZones.title: Find zones returns nothing
noZones.fix: The token's Zone Resources are set to no zone, or to zones this account cannot see. Edit them in Cloudflare and verify again.

nothingAppears.title: Connected, but no figures yet
nothingAppears.fix: Check that a zone is ticked. A verified token with no zone selected reads nothing, and the connection says so rather than looking healthy.

manage.title: Changing or removing it later
manage.intro: Everything is reversible from Settings → Cloudflare.
manage.disconnectDetail: The token and the zone selection are deleted together. Nothing is kept "for the history" — a stored secret you asked OpsWatch to forget would be a secret it did not forget. Reconnect by pasting a new token.

ai.title: Connect an AI provider
ai.subtitle: Optional. OpsWatch is complete without one.

0.title: Observed evidence
0.detail: What OpsWatch recorded, with timestamps. Never inferred.

1.title: Correlations
1.detail: Two recorded facts close together, with the gap stated. Never a cause.

2.title: AI hypothesis
2.detail: A guess from a model, labelled as one, beside the evidence it used.

3.title: Suggested investigation
3.detail: What would settle it, so you can check rather than believe.

unlocks.title: What connecting a provider adds
unlocks.intro: A model that can read what OpsWatch already measured and say it in a sentence. It does not measure anything, decide anything, or change anything — grouping, severity, baselines and anomalies are computed by written formulas whether or not a provider is configured.

before.title: Before you start
before.intro: An account with one of the supported providers, and a decision about whether you want this at all.
before.needDetail: An API key from Anthropic or OpenAI, or the address of any endpoint that speaks the OpenAI chat format — including one you host yourself.
before.costDetail: Your provider's usual per-token charge, and only when somebody asks a question. Nothing runs on a schedule. A connection test costs a single token.

permissions.title: What OpsWatch sends, and what it does not
permissions.intro: Your question, and a bounded pack of evidence it already collected.
permissions.grantDetail: The eight worst open problems, five recent deployments, five error groups that changed, and how each family looks — over the last 24 hours, capped at 32 kB. Titles, counts and timestamps.
permissions.whyDetail: No database dump, no raw log lines, no AWS credentials, no account identifiers, and nothing outside the environment you asked about. The limits are applied when the pack is built, not checked afterwards.
permissions.guaranteeTitle: What the model is told it may not do
permissions.guaranteeDetail: Never state a number, a service or a time that is not in the evidence. Never say one thing caused another — only that two happened close together, and how close. Say when the evidence does not support an answer. It is reading your estate, not changing it: OpsWatch has no write access to your infrastructure or your code.

steps.title: Configuring it
steps.methodIntro: Five steps, and you can undo all of them with one button.

choose.title: Choose a provider
choose.purpose: So swapping later is a setting rather than a rewrite.
choose.body: Anthropic and OpenAI are configured by name. The third option, an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, is for a gateway or a model you host yourself — you supply the address, over https.

key.title: Paste your API key
key.purpose: It is the only credential this needs.
key.body: Open Settings → AI provider and paste it. Leaving the field empty keeps whatever is already stored, which is how you change the model without retyping the key.

store.title: How it is stored
store.purpose: So you know what an attacker would have to reach.
store.body: Encrypted with a key derived for this purpose alone, and never sent back to your browser. The function that builds a request to your provider is not given the key at all, so a proxy that logs request bodies cannot capture it.

test.title: Test the connection
test.purpose: A saved key is not a working key.
test.body: Press Test connection. OpsWatch makes a one-token call and records the result as connected, invalid or unavailable. Until it passes, the provider reads "Saved, not tested" everywhere — and Ask OpsWatch stays unavailable, because a capability is what you can use rather than what is stored.

ask.title: Ask a question
ask.body: Open Overview → Ask OpsWatch in any environment. The answer appears under a heading that calls it a hypothesis, with the problems, deployments and error groups it was built from listed beneath it, and the model named. If OpsWatch has not read the environment yet it refuses to ask rather than getting a confident answer about an estate nobody has looked at.

states.title: What good and not-quite-right look like
states.intro: This guide, the Integrations page and the Accounts page read the same state.
states.goodDetail: The key has been tested and passed. Ask OpsWatch appears at the end of the Overview menu, after every deterministic surface.
states.degradedDetail: A key is saved but untested, or its last test failed. Changing the model or the endpoint also returns it here: that is a different connection, and the old result says nothing about it.

failures.title: When it does not work
failures.intro: Your provider's own error text never reaches an OpsWatch page — some providers echo the key back in it — so failures are named in OpsWatch's words.

unauthorized.title: The provider refused the key
unauthorized.fix: Check it, or paste a new one. This also appears if OPSWATCH_SECRET changed since the key was stored, which makes it undecryptable: store it again.

rateLimited.title: The provider is rate-limiting the key
rateLimited.fix: Wait, or use a key with more headroom. OpsWatch sends one request per question and never runs one on a schedule.

refusedEndpoint.title: OpsWatch refused to call the address
refusedEndpoint.fix: A custom endpoint that resolves inside your network or to the cloud metadata service is refused before the request is made, and again on every redirect. Use a public https address.

noEvidence.title: "There is nothing to answer from"
noEvidence.fix: The collector has not read that environment yet. This is deliberate: asking a model anyway would produce a confident paragraph about an estate nobody has looked at.

timeout.title: The provider did not answer in time
timeout.fix: Thirty seconds is the limit. A very large model behind a slow gateway can exceed it; try a smaller one.

manage.title: Changing or removing it later
manage.intro: Everything is reversible from Settings → AI provider.
manage.disconnectDetail: The key is deleted and the provider forgotten. Ask OpsWatch disappears from the menu and every other page works exactly as it did — which is the point of AI being optional rather than merely switchable.

Without keys, an AWS_PROFILE set in the shell that starts OpsWatch must name a profile that exists and can be read.

synthetics.title: Synthetics
synthetics.description: Checks OpsWatch runs from this host against your endpoints, on the collector’s schedule.

errors.invalid_threshold: A threshold is a whole number of milliseconds.

enables.github: Links a stack frame to the file it came from, and tells you which commits a deployment carried.
enables.ai: Optional. Lets a model narrate what OpsWatch already measured, for Ask OpsWatch and investigations.
enables.cloudflare: Traffic, cache and security events at the edge, for the zones you choose.
enables.google: Signing in with a Google account instead of a password.

access.aws: A read-only IAM role, ambient credentials, or access keys. The CloudFormation template lists every action it grants.
access.github: Repository contents, read-only. OpsWatch never writes to your code and has no code that could.
access.ai: Your API key, used only for questions you ask. OpsWatch is complete without it.
access.cloudflare: An API token scoped to the zones you pick, read-only.

detail.awsConnected: {accounts, plural, one {# account connected} other {# accounts connected}}
detail.awsFailing: {failing} of {accounts} cannot be read right now
detail.githubConnected: {repositories, plural, =0 {no repositories recorded yet} one {# repository} other {# repositories}}
detail.githubNoToken: {repositories, plural, =0 {no repositories recorded yet} one {# repository} other {# repositories}} — no token, so file contents cannot be read

Connect.signInHint: Google is an authentication provider, not something OpsWatch reads from. It is configured in the environment rather than here, and the Integrations page shows whether it is on.
